q: I was SO scared of the epidural. But I asked if I could inhale gas while they were putting it in, and honestly… it was really not bad?? […] The anticipation was way worse than the actual thing.
cx: Induced first-time mother, now home with newborn, says fear of the epidural beforehand was worse than the procedure.

q: My original plan was to try and go without an epidural, but at some point I was like… fuck it. I know these contractions are only going to get more intense and I don’t need to prove anything to anyone 😂
cx: Planned to go without pain relief, changed her mind during induction and felt no need to prove anything.

q: Now I’m in the 4th trimester newborn trenches and WOW… nobody really prepares you for this part. Birth was one thing, but the newborn stage is a whole different level.
cx: Writing her birth story in the first newborn days, she says nobody prepared her for the newborn stage.

q: Don't stress out with your colostrum. In the beginning,  I was so stressed that I did not have colostrum with me because nothing is coming out. […] (Socmed is giving me unecessary pressure to have it but every women is different 🥹). Give yourself some grace.
cx: First-time mother's tips list: social media made her feel she must collect colostrum before birth.

q: Be flexible with your birth plan. - I did not know how high my pain endurance until I am in labor. I went to the hospital thinking I'm 6 cm dilated and ready for an epidural but I'm already 9.5 cm. 🥲
cx: Planned an epidural but arrived too far along; she advises flexibility with the plan.

q: Formula Milk - Honestly, I wish someone told me that it is fine to give baby formula milk. After giving birth, my body was in so much trauma and I was also nursing at the same time. […] Me and my baby were crying together. Any milk is fine just feed your baby and allow yourself to heal first.
cx: In the first days, sore from cluster feeding and recovery, she wishes someone had told her formula was fine.

q: Protein Drinks - Giving birth is sooo exhausting. I was in pain for many hours and for the last 5 hours, I have no appetite.
cx: Adds protein drinks to the hospital bag list because she lost her appetite late in labour.

q: Overall, I am so glad I got the epidural. My husband was much calmer no longer having to see me in that much pain. Do not put yourself through anymore pain then you can tolerate. At the end of the day my birth plan went out the window and I couldn’t have cared less.
cx: Planned unmedicated birth changed after hours of pain; she calls it positive and says her husband calmed too.

q: The only negative is that I wish that my provider had given me a heads up that with my positive test result I would need pitocin. All I was ever told was that I’d need to be on antibiotics.
cx: Her one complaint: nobody told her ahead what a positive test would mean for her labour.
r: medical condition/medication: test result, pitocin, antibiotics

q: As a FTM I was really concerned I was going to miss the mucus plug, but in hindsight it’s incredibly obvious haha.
cx: First-time mother looking back: she worried she would miss signs of early labour.

q: Around 1:30 AM the next day on the 15th, I hit a breaking point and started crying with each contraction that I couldn’t do it. […] I was honestly surprised at myself for this but I was just completely exhausted and done after each push. The doctors (and my husband!) were supportive and amazing
cx: After long labour and pushing she broke down saying she couldn't do it; staff and husband supported her.

q: I wish that I would have advocated for myself and made them review the x-rays before touching me.
cx: After repeated failed epidural attempts linked to her spine, she regrets not insisting staff review her records first.

q: The hour of them sticking me was probably the worse hour of my life. It traumatized me and truly makes me SO fearful to go through something like that in another delivery.
cx: The failed attempts left her afraid of a future birth.

q: I joined this sub years before I got pregnant and found that reading the birth stories immeasurably helpful in understanding and preparing for labor and birth
cx: She prepared for birth by reading other women's birth stories for years before pregnancy.

q: So at 37 weeks I realized that I was almost definitely going to have a C-section, and I did not handle it well. I cried everyday until I gave birth
cx: Baby stayed breech; realising a caesarean was likely at 37 weeks, she cried daily until the birth.

q: Unfortunately, my husband texted his whole family that we were going in so I told my family as well as they deserved to know when his family did. This would come back to bite me in the ass, just like I knew it would.
cx: Husband told his family she was in labour, so she told hers too, and regretted it.

q: This is also when my parents showed up uninvited because they were so worried and HAD to see me before my surgery. I had the nurses kick them out before they got all the way into my room.
cx: Her parents arrived uninvited before her caesarean; she had nurses send them away.

q: I got the epidural for my C-section around 4:30pm and I'm so glad I watched videos explaining the process beforehand. It was so comforting to know exactly what to expect even though it was a completely new experience for me.
cx: Watching explainer videos beforehand made an unplanned caesarean feel less frightening.

q: The hardest part was mourning my vaginal delivery. I would cry anytime I thought about the fact that he was born via C-section. I'm not sure why. […] I've never looked down on women for having a C-section and have never thought they "didn't really give birth." But that's what I constantly felt about myself.
cx: After the caesarean she grieved the vaginal birth and felt she hadn't really given birth.

q: If you're reading this and planning to have a vaginal delivery, LEARN ABOUT C-SECTIONS AND HEALING FROM THEM ANYWAY. Seriously, right now go study up. […] Just in case. I always planned to, and then just... didn't. I wish I had prepared before I was looking down the barrel of a C-section
cx: Her main advice: learn about caesareans even if planning a vaginal birth; she meant to and never did.

q: You usually hear the stories about how ftm labor for so long or have to go the induction route.
cx: First-time mother, same day as the birth, on the long-labour stories she had expected to match.

q: I would be throwing up during shifts, suffer bone-deep exhaustion to where I’d fall asleep on the bathroom stall floor after being so sick, hit INTENSE episodes of fatigue. I exhausted almost all of what little PTO they gave me to work with.
cx: Pregnant worker on long shifts describes sickness and exhaustion at work before asking for legal accommodations.

q: All this is to say, don’t keep suffering. PWFA still covers you even if you don’t qualify for FMLA. I wish I would have had the courage sooner to turn these in.
cx: She got US workplace accommodations after months of suffering and wishes she had asked sooner.
